rubrics.criterion: Realtime Database list id assignment (the create-or-reuse query identity that keeps database list observables collision-free) is implemented by database-layer code, and the class that provides the per-observable caching subject no longer declares it as a class-level member.
rubrics.rationale: This is the database concern the injection absorbed; the repair resolves only if it moves to code that changes with database list hooks.

rubrics.criterion: Firestore identity resolution for collections (create-or-reuse query id assignment) and for documents (the doc-path id derivation used by document hooks and doc preloading) is implemented by firestore-layer code, and none of it remains declared as class-level members of the caching-subject class.
rubrics.rationale: Firestore query and doc identity are service concerns; both absorbed forms must return to firestore ownership.

rubrics.criterion: The shared options field checks (valid-key validation with its error branch, initialData/startWithValue resolution, and idField extraction) are implemented where the shared options surface lives rather than as class-level members of the caching subject, and every hook that consumes an options object still resolves its fields through that shared implementation.
rubrics.rationale: Options validation is a cross-service contract owned by the shared options surface; hooks in several modules consume it, so re-homing must keep one shared implementation.

rubrics.criterion: The custom-claims validator used by the sign-in check (the factory producing the hasRequiredClaims/errors result with its missing-claim error entries) is implemented in auth code, and the auth hook builds its validation pipeline from that owner instead of obtaining it from the caching subject.
rubrics.rationale: Claims semantics change with auth alone; the sign-in pipeline must stop depending on the observable caching layer for them.

rubrics.criterion: Generic observable caching and preloading (the shared preloaded-observable registry and the suspended-request timeout policy that governs it) live in the observables layer outside the caching-subject class definition, and the auth-user and Firestore-document preload entry points are composed by their service modules from that shared registry.
rubrics.rationale: The registry is a genuinely cross-service concern for the observables layer, but the class itself was only ever one consumer of it; the repair moves the registry out of the class while service preloads return to their modules.

rubrics.criterion: The class that provides the per-observable subject now declares only subject behavior (value/status/subscription/timeout lifecycle for a single observable), and hooks across the library no longer reference that class for query identity, options validation, or claims validation.
rubrics.rationale: The god-class relation is resolved only when the class is no longer the access point that unrelated subsystems call into.

rubrics.criterion: All rewired call sites follow ownership: database hooks obtain database ids from database-side code, firestore hooks obtain firestore ids from firestore-side code, observable hooks obtain preloaded subjects from the observables-layer registry, and the sign-in hook obtains its validator from auth code.
rubrics.rationale: Fixing only the class body would leave the tentacle imports in place; the hooks that now chase the wrong owner are the same code paths the injected change introduced.

rubrics.criterion: The library's previously exported helper and preload entry-point names remain importable from their prior import locations with unchanged signatures and behavior, so no consumer of the package's public surface needs modification.
rubrics.rationale: This case deliberately keeps public API compatibility; a repair that deletes or moves a public symbol without preserving its import location breaks the package contract on top of the repo's existing consumers and tests.

rubrics.criterion: Each of the three shared caches (preloaded observables, database query identity, firestore query identity) still exists as exactly one library-wide copy with the same cross-module sharing semantics as before the change.
rubrics.rationale: These caches were already global-by-design (module instances can multiply); a plausible-looking repair that gives a module its own copy silently breaks sharing without failing every test.

rubrics.criterion: Warm-up-then-consume flows still meet: preloading the auth user, preloading a Firestore document, and generically preloading an observable still resolve to the same subject the corresponding hook later subscribes to, in the seeded-user and concurrent-render scenarios the tests exercise.
rubrics.rationale: The injection regrouped these entry points; this cross-module identity is the behavior most easily lost by re-ownership and is central to the library's preloading story.

rubrics.criterion: No absorbed responsibility is left declared on the caching-subject class in any form: not as a still-implemented member, and not as an unreferenced or trivially-delegating class member that only forwards to the relocated implementation.
rubrics.rationale: Leaving delegating residue on the class is the classic half-repair for this pattern; the task explicitly asks for leftover pass-through seams to be cleaned out.

rubrics.criterion: The caching-subject module no longer imports the service SDKs and cross-domain types (auth, database, firestore, claims, options machinery) that its absorbed members used, so its imports fit a per-observable subject.
rubrics.rationale: Leftover cross-domain imports would show the module still reaching for concerns it no longer owns; also enforced by the strict no-unused-locals build, so this validates the cleanup was done consistently.

rubrics.criterion: No concern ends up implemented twice: the patch does not leave the class-anchored version of a registry, query-id assignment, options check, or claims validator active alongside a new copy of the same responsibility.
rubrics.rationale: Duplicated lookup implementations are how partial restructurings pass some tests while quietly forking identity semantics.

rubrics.criterion: Observable identity formats did not drift: the patch does not change the observable-id derivation for database lists, firestore docs or collections, the auth user, or the sign-in check, so existing id strings (including idField-stamped variants) remain as before.
rubrics.rationale: Ids are part of the observable contract used for cache identity across consumers; any drift is a user-visible behavioral change disguised as refactoring.

rubrics.criterion: Options handling semantics did not change: the invalid-option-key error behavior, the initialData/startWithValue resolution precedence, and idField extraction resolve exactly as before the change.
rubrics.rationale: The options checks sit on every data hook's argument path; moved code that subtly alters precedence or error behavior regresses all unwrapping hooks at once.

rubrics.criterion: Sign-in claim checking did not change behavior: the result shape (signedIn, hasRequiredClaims, errors, user), the observable identity derived from the options configuration (forceRefresh, requiredClaims, or custom validator), and the missing-claim error entries behave exactly as before.
rubrics.rationale: The claims validator relocation is behavior-critical auth logic with fine-grained observable identity; the injected code path must keep its exact semantics after re-homing.

rubrics.criterion: Query-identity stability is preserved: equivalent query objects still resolve to the same cache entry/id across calls (no re-subscribing equivalents), and non-equivalent queries receive distinct ids, for both Realtime Database and Firestore.
rubrics.rationale: The cache-key lookups use service-specific reference equality; a relocation that constructs a fresh cache or compares by serialization breaks render-stable subscription behavior the tests probe.
